en.justification: The town grew up around a royal homestead, at the crossroads of busy trading routes. Its present appearance dates to the second half of the 16th century, when the chateau was rebuilt as the seat of the provincial governor.

This unique square, hemmed in by burgher houses, shows the application of Baroque urban planning systems and decor. The complex comprises the Holy Trinity Column, the Jesuit college, parish church, the governor’s castle and fountains, representing a typical urban-planning project for a town.

Construction of the column began in 1700 opposite the house of the burgher, Z. Hodová, whose inheritance financed the project. The burgher’s legacy inspired other inhabitants to demonstrate similar civic generosity, and their donations paid for many of the sculptures that furnish the town, including in the Chapel of the Virgin Mary.

Entering from the square, a mighty stone gateway opens into a vaulted vestibule, a “*mázhaus*”; the gateway of which takes up almost two-thirds of its width. The *mázhaus*, used for the sale of hand-crafted luxury items and beer, has stairs leading to the cellar and upper floors, and a passageway to the yard and garden.

In the aftermath of the destruction caused by the earthquake of 1755, downtown Lisbon was rebuilt to comply with the innovative and pragmatic principles of Enlightenment urban planning and architecture.

With a square that opens up on to the river a new urban solution employing symbolic iconography was conceived. The rebuilding programme reaffirmed architecturally the absolute power of the king, principally through grand governmental and administrative buildings, a triumphal arch and a central-standing equestrian statue of King José I.
The uniform, multi-storey façades (with shops, three residential floors and an attic) are unique. They were constructed at a time when the focus was on safety and cost was a priority.

The symmetrical structure, built from wood, distributes and balances the forces of an earthquake. All buildings in downtown Lisbon were built according to the Gaiolas system, the world’s first anti-seismic structure.
This work of a bourgeois painter, a member of the St. Lucas Brotherhood, shows the outstanding Portuguese historical buildings in Belém and presents a chronicle of 17th-century Lisbon.

The Holy Trinity, standing in front of the Parish Church of the Holy Virgin and the Old Town House, is a typical feature of baroque urban planning. Different types of Holy Trinity statues reminded people of all those who had suffered during the plague of 1691.

The column celebrates the Church and the Christian tradition of the city. The work, undertaken by several masters of city architecture, is one of the last memorial columns to be built in several towns from the second half of the 17th century onwards under the Habsburg monarchy.
The sculpture at the top is of Christ the Saviour and God the Father, the ruler of the world, which opens out from the figure of the Archangel Michael, the symbol of the eternal struggle with heresy.

Light played a major role in Baroque iconography as a symbol of the Holy Spirit. Angels, as mediators of God’s will and messengers and guardians of the light, are bringing holiness to the citizens of Olomouc.

The parish church, which commonly dominates the urban structure, was an important meeting point in the city both as a symbol representing its citizens and as a memorial monument. Churches named after St Jacob are dedicated to pilgrims and travelling merchants.

The high-altar of this church, built on one of Tyrol’s busiest market-squares, includes one of Austria’s most admired sacred pictures. The cult of Saint Jacob attracted both the city’s inhabitants as well as merchant travellers coming to do business in the city.
The church is the mausoleum of the archduke, whose residence was in the town, and a burial place for some of the city’s other noble inhabitants, as well as a memorial to them all.

The richly decorated pulpit includes personifications of the divine Virtues, who not only instructed the bourgeoisie in God’s word, but also provided a basic education while also offering new information about the world.

The noble woman, presented holding compasses in one hand, sits in front of sheets of drawing paper, a ruler and a protractor. At the time, geometry was considered a form of entertainment for amateurs and a part of what constituted a good education.
Wisdom was an important part of the city’s self-presentation.
The Observatory was created as part of the public Institute of Sciences and Arts.
The University of Coimbra library, dedicated to King João, is an important example of civil Baroque architecture.
The richly decorated tables correspond with the exclusivity of the books that are read as means to attain wisdom.
Manifestations of Wisdom present the importance of the *bibliotheca* (library) as of the *universitas* (university) of daily life.
New books on theology, philosophy and law were acquired with the university’s new curricula.
The bourgeois music master of the king’s court is dressed in a ceremonial court vestment, adorned with the prestigious Order.
The historian, custodian of the university library and an eminent scholar, commissioned the portrait directly from the artist.
The theme of the engraving is related to the brutality of the Inquisition.

This illumination represents a theatre-set in the shape of a ship. It was constructed on Bologna’s main square on the occasion of the Feast of the Roast Pork, August 1657, which every year attracted great numbers of people.
The model of the proposed theatre was exhibited at the town hall to allow all citizens the option to express an opinion about it.
This ambitious ensemble was the urban residence of the sculptor, Egid Quirin Asam. The iconological stucco-façade is connected with his endowment and creation of a church.
The painted houses are thus to be regarded as kind of status-symbols of the inhabitants, in this case, a merchant.
The house of this artistic family is decorated with sacred and allegorical fresco-paintings that are representative within the area.
The palace was erected to mark the election of a family member as Senator of the city.
The staircase played an important role in the representation ceremony.
In this allegory, the family is celebrated alongside the therapeutic capacities of the thermal springs at Porretta.
The representative first floor presents allegories of the “circle of life”.

Although oratories usually belong within a domestic context, they were also designed as portable furniture for religious purposes. This oratory-desk or cabinet-on-stand was designed for a ship, and belonged to the bourgeois family-owners of a glass and porcelain factory.
The oratory has black decorative tablets embellished with vegetal elements and gilded and lacquered panels holding iconographic motifs known as *chinoiserie*s.
The design and ornamentation are characteristic of the so-called King João V style.
The popularity of porcelain and lacquer wares resulted in specially designed halls in mansions and palaces that were furnished with bureau cabinets, such as this one, in which to display them.
The popularity of porcelain and lacquer wares resulted in specially designed halls in mansions and palaces that were furnished with bureau cabinets, such as this one, in which to display them.
The mirror-frame testifies to the great skill and the refined taste of Bolognese carvers, who looked to Rome and Venice, for the most up-to-date ideas.
The richly decorated bracket clock, from a manor near Varaždin, has a gilt-wood case decorated in the Rococo style.
A party of wealthy people are enjoying themselves in a grand park, perhaps part of the Gnudi country-house estate to which the painting originally belonged.
The small church was donated by citizens in the 1630s during a plague epidemic.
The Chapel of the Rosary was created in 1589 when the Brotherhood of the Rosary refurbished the medieval chapel that previously was held by the Guidotti family.
A family offered the Brotherhood of the Holy Body part of their palace to use as accommodation.
St. Elmo was the patron saint of the Brotherhood of Fishermen, Navigators and Ship Owners founded in the 14th century.
The main altar of the richly decorated chapel is the high point of the house.
The entrance staircase is richly decorated with *azulejos* (tiles) depicting welcoming figures, putti and vases of flowers.

The origin of the Church of St. Joseph’s – the patron saint of carpenters – is directly linked to local social conditions. In summer, when there was virtually no work for craftsmen, carpenters and other trades were forced to take to the road as journeymen. Church services, held on their departure and their return, were celebrated by the whole community in the guild church.

The painting depicts the Holy Family as the patron saint of the Brotherhood: Mary and Joseph in adoration of the Holy Trinity are presented with attributes and symbols of the guild (carpenter’s tools) by putti.
The suffering Christ, as the symbol of all suffering and humankind’s ability to overcome it, is presented to itinerant workers both as a token of consolation and as a warning.

The piece, placed near the triumphal arch of the Church of St. Mark in Zagreb, was commissioned by the Boot-makers Guild. The commission was made possible from a donation by Ana Gerlić, whose name can be seen on the coat-of-arms.
This painting, by a famous Baroque Slovenian painter, was commissioned for the altar of St. Mary Magdalene in the parish church of St. Mary in Zagreb and is dedicated to the Boot-makers Guild.

The aqueduct distributed water to the city of Lisbon. An open-air structure with monumental pointed arches, it included underground galleries, a reservoir, and other springs which endowed adjacent systems such as canals and fountains.
Due to its monumentality, the Mãe d'Água constitutes a true civic temple to *águas livres* (the free waters).
A secondary aqueduct spreads out, around the city of Lisbon, terminating in fountains. Many, like this one, are still extant.
The “show-fountain”, imitating a triumphal arch, was dedicated to Pope Paul V Borghese. It celebrates the great undertaking of bringing water from the Lake of Bracciano (about 40 km away) to Rome.
A series of fountains and columns, symbolising the rebirth of the city, demonstrates both the city’s historical significance and its affiliation to Christianity.

en.name: The Hercules fountain
en.justification: Reducing history to myth was typical both for the aristocracy and town organisations. The statue celebrates a legend associated with establishment of the town.
Mercury, the Roman god of trade, blesses the town's prosperity at the intersection of two streets close to the parish church, where the merchants, who were members of the nobility, are buried.
The fountain, dedicated to Neptune the god of water, is believed to protect the town from all of the watery elements.

The subject of the fountain is water as a source of life and a symbol of purity together with the ideals of good over evil and order over chaos, seen in the context of the power of Christianity and the Habsburg Empire. With this fountain, the City of Brno demonstrated its loyalty to the emperor while monumentalising the city’s place within European history.

“Art monuments”, of course, are associated with their clients and designers as well as builders and, sometimes, bureaucrats as well. Construction of the fountain was administered by the Senator of Brno, Dechau. He supervised the architect and managed the builders. He may be the person depicted explaining the fountain’s symbolism to a group of aristocrats.
The fountain stands on the site of an earlier monument in the city’s second most important square, at the intersection of one of its main communication routes.
Besides their devotion to providing healthcare in the local community, the Jesuits also had extensive worldwide experience in pharmacy-management owing to their missionary activities.
Pharmacists belonged to the city’s elite. They often held posts on the city council or, for example, acted as chroniclers.
At a time when many diseases and epidemics were rife, successful pharmacies were places of commerce, but were also known as centres of excellence in medical research and chemical experiments.

The hospital and church was an important part of the city’s infrastructure and both were places of charity. The main building served both as an administrative headquarters and hospital, with the attached church managed autonomously.

To visit the sick is one of the virtues, mercy. Mercy, as contemplated here, is said to be the virtue influencing one’s desire to have compassion for others and, if possible, to alleviate another’s misfortune.

The doctorial thesis was put up as a poster to invite academics, citizens and visitors to a public discussion. As well as depicting the principal patron saints of the land, the image presents personifications of a good reign, which were considered prerequisites for the country’s prosperity.
The Pauline monastery had a grammar school and was the first Academy awarded the right to confer doctorates.
The Croatian Jesuit, a leading physicist, mathematician, astronomer, philosopher and writer, taught mathematics in Rome.
Ratkay, who was from a noble family, was one of Croatia’s first cartographers. He had been a page at the court of Emperor Leopold I, studied philosophy and read law before becoming a Jesuit.
At the Jesuit grammar school the armillary sphere was used to teach the distances between planets and stars and to measure time.
The noble woman is probably a daughter of Laudivio Zacchia who, once widowed, gave his life to religion and was made a cardinal.
The former residence of the company’s directors and factory for Antverpian (Dutch) merchants is one of Rijeka city’s most representative buildings.
The Imperial-style staircase represents the company’s commercial ambitions.
Wall-decorations are inspired by Piranesi, whose work was disseminated through prints that were purchased by the nobility.
The harbour was an important trading place, but not only in exotic wares.
Exotic wares become prototypes for domestic workshop-production.
The decoration and the materials employed here are from Mughal (Indian) sources.
Probably the work of one of the numerous glass workshops on the island of Murano, near Venice, which were on sale throughout Europe.
The decoration of this vase, made in a Dutch workshop, is inspired by Oriental designs.
Commissioning of these vessels with Oriental motifs has been attributed to members of different Portuguese families.
The monumental and sumptuous villa of this noble family stands in the fertile countryside close to the city.
Triumphal motifs in stucco decorate the ballroom.
The magnificent ballroom occupying the centre of the villa.
Allegories of Time and Love decorate one of the richly decorated rooms.

The dynamism and elegance of the space, along with the changing views that can be enjoyed through the arcades and columns from the small loggia at the top of the stairs, are typical of a local Baroque architecture that owes most of its devices to the theatrical tradition.

The dynamism and elegance of the space, along with the changing views that can be enjoyed through the arcades and columns from the small loggia at the top of the stairs, are typical of a local Baroque architecture that owes most of its devices to the theatrical tradition.
Later villas were open to nature: a topographic view of the loggia reveals different viewpoints whether looking through its columns, balustrades or arcades.
The function of tapestries was not only aesthetic and symbolic but also practical, to maintain the room’s climate.
Next to landscapes, still-life was the most admired interior decoration.

A portrait of a black slave or servant dressed in a noble, although poorly conserved clothes. The painting can also be viewed as a sort of genre painting, exploring images of the popular and picturesque in everyday life.
This kind of salon furnishing was popular among European bourgeois families until the second half of the 20th century.
The first floor of this palace, built above three houses a few metres from the main city-square, was decorated with scenes celebrating the family.
These splendid mythological scenes celebrate the good fortune of the family.
The epitaph ensures that Anna Kun is still remembered by society.
The figure of a “distinguished bourgeois” gentleman from a small town is accompanied by an angel announcing the choices he has to face: the world he is looking to or eternity.
The rich collection of paintings donated by wealthy parishioners is exceptional, and should be seen as votive gifts to the Protestant Church.
The rich collection of paintings donated by wealthy parishioners is exceptional, and should be seen as votive gifts to the Protestant Church.
The rich collection of paintings donated by wealthy parishioners is exceptional, and should be seen as votive gifts to the Protestant Church.

This is an example of a typical civic picture depicting St. Florian as the defender against fire. As one of the most popular saints in Central Europe, he is the subject of many sculptures and paintings.
The church and monastery were designed and built through a donation of the municipal physician on the occasion of the plague-year, 1611.
The church and monastery were designed and built through a donation of the municipal physician on the occasion of the plague-year, 1611.
The curious symbolic architecture is crowned by a tower that expresses the motif of the Trinity.
Decoration of the gallery, comprising allegorical and heraldic figures, alludes to the city’s history; its greatness, good government and “virtues”.
The ceiling-painting symbolises the power of the city.

The tower clock, embellished with several chronological devices and much pictorial symbolism, is integral to the town hall. The allegorical scenes demonstrate the significance of Olomouc as the seat of the bishopric and the one-time centre of the country.
The town hall, the administrative centre of the city, also had chambers that included representative rooms.
The ceremonial hall was designed for meeting the *Landtag* (state diet).

The town hall of a province or city included, beside the administrative rooms, the bread store, the city’s *vinotheque* for wine storage, and a representative hall that hosted a diversity of festivities.
Image-based programmes proclaimed the virtues of the city’s regimental success.

These paintings, which hang in the library’s principle room, celebrate native men who became famous in various fields (i.e., literature, politics, sciences and the arts); many of them also play a part in the city’s socio-political history.

Justice was an important part of the city’s iconography. Judges belonged to the city’s nobility and also played a part in government. As a result of his work this city judge amassed a large sum of money with which he supported the foundation of a school.
The soldiers are distributed in two companies of fusiliers and grenadiers. The company includes hunters, musicians, guards, a canteen and a surgeon, as well as non-commissioned officers.

A descendant of a noble and distinguished Croatian family, Zrinski excelled in battle against the Turkish forces and was made a count. The painting was commissioned for a Pauline monastery. Zrinski is also known for his literary works.
The fortress belongs to the west wing of a large system of Baroque fortress-towns, which were constructed at the Danube node, on the border with the Turkish Empire.
The fortress complex with the church in the centre was designed to accommodate 4,000 soldiers.
The Foscolo Arch, the biggest public monument in Korčula, is dedicated to General Leonardo Foscolo who was a military commander of Venetian Dalmatia.

The monument of General Luigi Ferdinando Marsili is in the Church of St. Dominic in Bologna, conveying perfectly the Baroque theme of Fame defeating Time. Marsili supplemented his training by studying mathematics, anatomy and natural history with the best teachers and through personal observation. After a course of scientific studies in his native city, he travelled throughout the Ottoman Empire collecting data on both its military organisation and natural history.
This residence of a Lieutenant-colonel of the cavalry troops was the meeting place of the city’s elite and a venue for theatrical performances and concerts.
Initially the Barberini were based in Florence, where they were landowners, before they became successful merchants.

The palace, which blends in with the ancient Roman remains, has decorative antique motifs that are employed as symbols of the owner’s status and an investment in his overall self-promotion and legitimating.

Two central flights of stairs in the *cavea* together with the installation of the well give the palace the character of an urban development, which is underlined by the fusion between the ancient and modern structures.
Both the inscription on the main portal and the coat-of-arms on the well are evidence of the significant number of works commissioned by the Colonna family.
The Pamphili family, originally from a small Umbrian patriciate, found recognition of its social ascent with the appointment to the papacy of Giovanni Battista (Innocent X).
Along with the church and the piazza, the palazzo constitutes the hinge of the urban layout of the recently re-designed “città panfilia”, commissioned by Camillo Pamhili.

The Valmontone estate was acquired by the nephew of Pope Innocent X with the aim of undertaking a grand restructuring project of the entire village, which was to be centred round the palace, the church and the square.
Built on a site previously occupied by medieval houses, the palace was the residence of a family whose members were part of the city’s Senate.
In celebration of himself this nobleman inaugurated a new interior staircase to lead guests up to the noble floor where the ballroom was situated.
The painted figures are based on antique statues.
The villa, while typical of Baroque residential architecture in Dubrovnik during the period, is also very innovative.
A fine and well-preserved example of bourgeois Rococo representation and contemporary domestic culture, the palace was built for a financier.
Already, on the staircase, the visitor is reminded of the profession, rank, and claim to power of the family.
Commissioned by a rich merchant, the palace was part of the programme for the city’s improvement.
This memorable banquet was documented by a series of printed etchings and descriptions.
Seeking contentedness by drinking and smoking – seen as the minor pleasures of life – was often depicted as a warning to the viewer about how the pleasures of life turn into indulgence.
This richly decorated console was probably used to display rare and fine tableware.
The history of the Croatian border troops is depicted on this renowned Meissen-manufactory ware.
The history of the Croatian border troops is depicted on this renowned Meissen-manufactory ware.
The history of the Croatian border troops is depicted on this renowned Meissen-manufactory ware.
The history of the Croatian border troops is depicted on this renowned Meissen-manufactory ware.
These kinds of products from the Buda workshop were extremely popular among the Hungarian bourgeoisie and aristocracy of the late 18th century.

The symbolic objects and food commonly associated with the Eucharist are set out on the table according to the strict ceremonial rules and etiquette of this very special feast day. The ceramics, however, allude to the daily simplicity of a small Portuguese society.

Expensive tableware and excessively adorned tables represent the sins of lust and vanity which are seen as symbols of transience; alternatively, the peonies allude to salvation and chastity while other flowers depicted symbolise purity, patience and martyrdom.
This still-life is the only known work of a remarkable artist of Spanish descent, Ximenes. In 1698 he became a burgher of Brno in Moravia and an active member of the Painters Guild.
This painting is typical of a burgher-painter, depicting the influence of Dutch and Italian still-life painting.
The crests of two important families decorate this ornate silver book-cover. Unfortunately it is not known why it was commissioned.
The coat-of-arms, as part of the decoration of this mirror-frame, belongs to a German merchant who was part of an industrialist family from Croatia.
An example of a popular Moravian design the shape and decoration of which is based on Rococo *faience* following the tradition of Habán ceramics.

Many of the Habáns, forced to leave Moravia after the Battle of White Mountain in 1620, settled in the adjacent territory of western Slovakia. Here, they gradually became assimilated into the local Catholic population.
Habán potters returned to Moravia in the last quarter of the 17th century to practice their craft under more favourable conditions. The tradition of “folk *faience*” in Moravia dates to this period.

With the escalating social whirl of the 18th century, people’s actions and the relationships between them, especially conversation between men and women – a subject matter originating in 17th-century Dutch burgher culture – became increasingly popular.
